q: Top-down merge sort (split into ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉) is run on 8 distinct elements. What is the maximum number of element comparisons it can make?
explain:
A merge producing k elements uses at most k − 1 comparisons.

4 merges of 1+1 → 4 × 1 = 4
2 merges of 2+2 → 2 × 3 = 6
1 merge of 4+4  → 1 × 7 = 7
total worst case = 17

In general, the worst case is n⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2^⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 = 8·3 − 8 + 1 = 17.

q: How many inversions (pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]) does the array [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] have?
explain: Every pair is inverted in a strictly decreasing array, so there are C(5, 2) = 5·4/2 = 10 inversions. This is the maximum for 5 elements.

q: Solve the recurrence T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log n.
explain: n^(log₄ 3) ≈ n^0.79, and f(n) = n log n is polynomially larger (by n^0.21 or more). The regularity condition holds: 3·(n/4)·log(n/4) ≤ (3/4)·n log n. So case 3 gives T(n) = Θ(f(n)) = Θ(n log n).

q: Which statements about merge sort are true?
options: Its worst-case time is Θ(n log n)
It sorts an array in place with O(1) extra memory
It is well suited to sorting linked lists and huge files stored on disk
explain:
(A) and (B) are standard. (D): merging only needs sequential access, which is ideal for linked lists and for external sorting of data too big for memory.

(C) is false: array merge sort needs Θ(n) extra space.
